topic: The Invisible Bridge: Connecting Integrals and Derivatives
target_audience: First-year university students or Advanced Placement (AP) Calculus students

sections.title: The Concept of 'Inverse' Operations
sections.content: Introduce the idea that many mathematical operations have a 'reverse' partner. This sets the stage for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus by relating it to familiar concepts like addition/subtraction and multiplication/division.
sections.example: Imagine a 'Mathematical Time Machine': if adding 5 moves a character 5 steps forward, subtracting 5 brings them back to the start. We will discover if the same exists for Calculus.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: The Derivative as a 'Rate'
sections.content: Briefly revisit the derivative as the instantaneous rate of change or the slope of a tangent line. Use a graphical representation of a curve where a moving point shows the changing slope.
sections.example: An animation of a car driving up a hill: the speedometer shows the 'Derivative' (velocity) at every specific point on the slope.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: The Integral as 'Accumulation'
sections.content: Define the definite integral as the area under a curve. Visualize this by filling the space under a velocity-time graph with thin rectangles (Riemann sums) that merge into a solid color.
sections.example: A 'Digital Rain Gauge': as rain falls at varying intensities (the function), the total water collected in the bucket represents the Integral (the area/accumulation).

sections.title: The Bridge: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
sections.content: Explain the core relationship: Differentiation and Integration are inverse processes. If you integrate a function and then differentiate the result, you return to the original function.
sections.example: Display the equation d/dx [ ∫ f(t) dt ] = f(x). Show a 'Function Factory' where a raw material goes through an 'Integrator' machine and then a 'Differentiator' machine, coming out exactly as it started.

sections.title: Visualizing the Connection: The Area Function
sections.content: Animate a moving vertical line (x) that 'paints' the area under a curve f(t). Show that the rate at which this area grows at any moment is exactly equal to the height of the function at that point.
sections.example: A 'Growing Carpet' animation: As a character unrolls a carpet (the area), the speed at which the carpet area increases is determined by the width of the roll (the function's value f(x)).

sections.title: Real-World Application: The Racing Cheetah
sections.content: Apply the concept to physics. If we know the velocity (derivative of position), we can find the total distance (integral). Conversely, if we have the distance, we can find the velocity.
sections.example: A Cheetah sprints. Graph 1 (Velocity): The area under the curve shows the Cheetah moved 100 meters. Graph 2 (Position): The slope of this line at 3 seconds matches the height of Graph 1 at 3 seconds.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Recap the 'Inverse' relationship. Emphasize that the integral allows us to find the 'net change' by knowing the 'rate of change', and vice versa.
sections.example: Final split-screen: Left side shows 'Slope Calculation' (Derivative), right side shows 'Area Calculation' (Integral), with a bridge connecting them labeled 'Calculus'.
